prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is only one result so far. The starting network scored 0.000 and collapsed to ending with DONE immediately. By 50% of training, episodes were 1.0 step long. The likely cause is the hidden mirror rule. A brick chosen at column x lands at column X-dx-x. The starting network is a local, translation-equivariant CNN with a receptive field of about 5 cells, so it cannot connect the place where a brick is needed to the far-off action column that would put it there. Almost every placement scores negative, so DONE (reward 0) wins and the policy collapses. Flipping a learned feature map along x lines up each action anchor with its true landing footprint, including the dx-1 shift, when pooled over the footprint. Giving the head both the normal and flipped feature maps keeps that choice learned. This round tests: (1) the head reads both orientations; (2) a learned column-mixing layer that must discover the mirror itself; (3) option 1 with more, smaller updates and more entropy to resist the DONE collapse.

### Round 2
The mirror rule is the main obstacle. Without help the starting network learned nothing (0.00). Giving the pool head a flipped copy of the features worked: r1c1 reached 0.70. Making it learn the column remap itself was much worse (r1c2, 0.10), so RL could not find the permutation within this budget. Doubling the number of updates (n_envs 128) and raising entropy to 0.02 lifted the score to 0.90 (r1c3). Its two seeds differ by 3 points, which is about the seed noise. Training success was still rising at the end (0.77 at 75% of training, 0.88 at 100%), so the budget limits learning, and the recipe is the main lever. This round tests two ways to get more out of the budget: fewer PPO epochs (more samples) and more frequent updates. It also tests a cleaner design that flips the whole trunk into landing coordinates right after the learned 1x1 stem. That keeps all features aligned with where bricks land and drops the doubled head input.

### Round 3
Lining the network up with the mirror rule (flipping features along x) did most of the work: dev success went from 0 to 0.70. Going from 32 to 64 updates took it to 0.90. After that, three variants all scored about 0.92-0.93: 2 PPO epochs (0.921), flipping the whole trunk (0.922) and 128 updates (0.928). Seeds differ by up to about 0.03, so these three are tied. Training success levels off near 0.87 and very few cells land outside the target (0.27 per episode). In r2c3's failed diagnostic trace the agent filled a cell under an overhang that had to stay empty. So the remaining errors look like overhang and ordering mistakes, which need wider spatial context, not more updates. Plan: one control that combines 2 epochs with 64 worlds (about 236 updates). Two tests use the same recipe and add one network change each: a deeper, wider trunk (7x7 receptive field) and a whole-board summary added back into the trunk.

### Round 4
Lining the features up with the mirrored landing columns was the decisive change. Without it the starting network scored 0. A fixed flip scored 0.70 to 0.93, and a learned column remap reached only 0.10. After that, the recipe mattered most. Going from 32 to 64 updates raised success from 0.70 to 0.90. r2c3 (flipped trunk, 64 worlds, 4 epochs, about 128 updates) is best at 0.928. r2c1 (2 epochs, 128 worlds) and r2c2 (flipped trunk, 64 updates) both scored about 0.92, the same within noise. In round 3, every run that used 2 epochs with 64 worlds (about 236 small updates) collapsed to DONE on both seeds, or nearly so. That includes the deeper-trunk and global-context runs, so those two ideas were never properly tested. Their recipe was the confound. Safe recipes so far use at least about 2k samples per update or 4 epochs. Remaining errors are probably wrong ordering under overhangs or stopping at the wrong time (IoU 0.989 against 0.92 success).

name: flipped trunk, 128 updates
